title: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
hookLine: the call to prayer, and why it's beautiful even if you don't know the words
last: AS-SIRAT AL-MUSTAQIM — SHOW US THE WAY.

cards: Before dawn, in a city still dark, one voice starts up from a minaret. A single voice, rising, holding a note longer than seems possible, then falling away. Then a second voice, farther off, a beat behind.
Then another. For a few minutes the rooftops are full of the same words, never quite in sync. It isn't a song, exactly, and it isn't an alarm.
It's an invitation, sent out at each of the five prayer times.

teach.h: ADHAN — FROM THE ROOT FOR EAR.
teach.b: The adhan. Its root, a-dh-n, is the root of the ear, udhun: the call is literally the thing you hear. In the first years in Medina, the sayings report, the young community didn't have one.
People gathered by guessing the time. The companions talked it over: a bell? A horn?
A fire? Then a companion named Abdullah ibn Zayd dreamed of a man teaching him the words.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said it was a true dream, and told him: teach it to Bilal, his voice carries. Bilal is the man from day fifteen, saying ahad, one, under the rock.
By now he was free, and his voice called the city to prayer. The words: Allahu akbar, God is greater. Then two witnesses: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.

teach.h: COME TO PRAYER. COME TO SUCCESS.

teach.b: Hayya 'ala l-falah: come to success. Falah is flourishing, and its root is the root of the farmer, the one who splits the ground so something can grow. At dawn, Sunni callers add a line: prayer is better than sleep.
The Shia call carries a line of its own at every prayer: come to the best of deeds. That's why it can be beautiful even without the Arabic. Its whole job is to turn toward you and say: come.

how: In Muslim-majority places a mu'adhdhin gives the adhan from the mosque, often by loudspeaker, at each of the five prayer times; elsewhere it's often heard from an app, and in many families it's said softly into a newborn's ear.

games.q: what's inside the call — tap the pairs.
p: the voice the Prophet chose for the call

s: the first Muslims in Medina already had a call to prayer
at first they gathered by guessing the time; the call came after the companions talked it over.
the root of adhan is the root of the Arabic word for ear
a-dh-n: udhun, the ear. the call is the thing you hear.
every call to prayer uses exactly the same words everywhere
at dawn Sunni callers add prayer is better than sleep; the Shia call adds come to the best of deeds at every prayer.

games.q: you're one of the first Muslims in Medina. people keep missing the prayer. the options on the table: a bell, a horn, a fire. what does the community end up with?
games.why: a companion dreamed the words, and the Prophet said: teach them to Bilal, his voice carries. a person, calling people.

practice: Close your eyes and listen. Not to anything in particular: just to what's calling right now. A car outside, the fridge, your own breathing, someone's voice in another room.
Each one is asking for a little of your attention. Notice what you turn toward. If you pray, you can let the old words sit under the sound: come to prayer, come to success.

wordCard.voice: The adhan. The call to prayer, from the root for ear. God is greater; come to prayer; come to success. Seventeenth word.

orig.note: Arabic: the call to prayer, from a-dh-n, the root of udhun, the ear.

carryVoice: Your line: you are being called. Come to prayer, come to flourishing, said to you. Day seventeen.
